subject: Segmenting transects for DSM: are x, y fields required?

messages.author: 8fbbf490c07a1909
messages.subject: Segmenting transects for DSM: are x, y fields required?
parts:
Hi listfolk,

I realise I’ve missed something. Recent examples of segment level data include x and y fields calculated from the lats and long (e.g. using latlong2km function) that older segment level data for DSM did not have, while retaining the latitude and longitude fields.  As I’m currently in the process of segmenting data in preparation for DSM, I’ve been wondering:
  • Are the x, y fields necessary for DSM?
  • If you have the x, y fields, why retain latitude and longitude?
I think the following passage from Ch 5 of the users guide explains it partly (the later chapter on preparing data for DSM doesn’t seem to mention the x, y fields at all):

"Projecting data takes time. This can significantly affect the performance of survey design calculations, such as calculating coverage probability and creating new surveys. Therefore, if you always use the same external GIS package and storing the projected data in a shapefile. When you bring the data into Distance, set it as no coordinate system (you can do this by setting the coordinate system and projection to [None] in File | Project Properties | Geographic, and setting the units correctly, and then not copying over the .prj part of the shapefiles when you import your shapefiles – see Importing Existing GIS data). Distance will then treat the data as simple x,y coordinates and will not spend time projecting and re-projecting it."

So, is there anything I need to do in Distance 7.0b3 to tell it to use the computationally simpler x, y fields, or is enough to leave out the x, y fields and set the project properties to [None] for the coordinate system and projection?

Any answers appreciated!

Stewart

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Segmenting transects for DSM: are x, y fields required?
parts:
Stewart

Readers of this list who are not interested in georeferenced coordinates on the surface of the earth, look away now.

Yes, there have been a few changes to the example project of the Gulf of Mexico spotted dolphins; but I believe x and y have been present in the R example data since Miller et al. (2013) MEE paper described the analysis.  The standalone Distance project used latitude and longitude of segment centres, not taking account of the inequality of a degree of latitude and a degree of longitude.

There were two transformations performed upon both the segment and prediction grid data.  Remember any covariates that appear at the segment layer and subsequently used in your prediction model, will need to be present in your prediction grid.  Lat/long was converted to UTMs to solve the asymmetry of degrees of lat/long.  Secondly, Miller centred the UTMs on the centroid of the study area so the values were more compatible.  Notice that the vignette and wiki you cite in your email both use "x" and "y" and predictors having made these adjustments.  As such, the "latitude" and "longitude" variables are redundant and not used in the analyses, and could have been deleted.

If you are working with a small-ish study area, then lat/long is probably not a sensible coordinate system in which to record your data.  The modest GIS inside standalone Distance can transform lat/long to UTMs, but it cannot centre the coordinates.  Centring is unlikely to make vast differences to your analysis, but because spatial models can do curious things, centring provides some protection from some of those curiosities.
